entities.summary:
Kaṇāda, also known by his epithets Kaṇabhaksha and Kaṇabhuj, was a pivotal ancient Indian natural scientist and philosopher credited with founding the Vaisheshika school of Indian philosophy around the 6th to 2nd century BCE, with 160 BCE often cited for his death. His work represents one of the earliest systematic formulations of atomism in human history, independent of contemporary Greek thought. Operating within the vibrant intellectual landscape of ancient India, Kaṇāda’s contributions laid the groundwork for a unique understanding of the physical world, emphasizing empirical observation and logical inference, which profoundly shaped subsequent Indian scientific and philosophical discourse.

The core of Kaṇāda’s Vaisheshika system centers on the concept of *anu* (atom) as the indivisible, eternal building blocks of the universe. He posited six categories of reality (*padarthas*): substance (*dravya*), quality (*guna*), action (*karma*), generality (*samanya*), particularity (*vishesha*), and inherence (*samavaya*). His meticulous classification sought to explain the diversity and interactions of the material world, asserting that all complex objects are aggregates of these fundamental atoms, which possess inherent qualities and combine in specific ways. This rigorous analytical framework, articulated in his seminal text, the *Vaisheshika Sutra*, provided a sophisticated proto-physical theory that aimed to understand existence through its constituent elements and their properties.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Kaṇāda's pioneering work in establishing the Vaisheshika school and its atomic theory profoundly shaped Indian philosophy and science for over a millennium, influencing a major intellectual tradition that integrated with Nyaya. His systematic classification of reality provided an early and independent framework for understanding the physical universe.
